{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nv-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"8113ba0738899ee10a9ce8a22be7399ad166f0d58cd031e26ed8af10ef1b5285","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:41","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","source_liveness_sha256":"0dfbf3aa4b4798b88d69252e076642b5f0a38751c5010711fbce93c8a7d6e292"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Towing with a Class C license: limits, loading, hitching, inspection, backing, turning, clearance and combination vehicles","heading":"C — Towing: what a Class C license may tow, weight terms, loading and balance, ball and fifth-wheel hitches, trailer inspection, towing safely, backing with a trailer, turns, space around the rig, combination vehicles and trailer skids","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Towing: what a Class C license may tow, weight terms, loading and balance, ball and fifth-wheel hitches, trailer inspection, towing safely, backing with a trailer, turns, space around the rig, combination vehicles and trailer skids
Knowledge domain: the weight and length a non-commercial Class C driver may tow, the weight ratings that matter, how to load and balance a trailer, what to check when hitching a ball coupler or fifth-wheel trailer, when to re-inspect on a trip, how backing and turning change with a trailer, how to judge space above and below, and how combination vehicles skid and roll.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
A non-commercial Class C driver may tow a single vehicle or a combination as long as its gross vehicle weight rating does not exceed 10,000 pounds and the whole unit is 70 feet long or shorter. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
Drivers who want more towing information, or a J endorsement, should read the Nevada Non-Commercial A and B, J Endorsement Study Guide on the DMV website. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
Loading a trailer wrongly endangers you and others, since loose items can strike other road users and a quick stop or crash can damage the trailer's interior. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
Overloading hurts steering, braking and speed control: an overloaded rig crawls up hills, gains too much speed downhill, needs longer to stop, and its overworked brakes can fail. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
Gross vehicle weight is the total weight of one vehicle plus its load, while gross combination weight is the total of the powered unit, its trailer or trailers, and the load. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
Gross combination weight rating is the manufacturer's stated combined loaded weight for a vehicle and the vehicle it tows. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
A tire's load rating, printed on its sidewall, is the most weight it can carry safely at a stated pressure; suspensions and coupling devices also carry maximum weight ratings. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A02
The higher a load's center of gravity, the more likely the vehicle is to overturn, so keep cargo as low as possible and put the heaviest items underneath or in lower compartments. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A02
Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard and can damage that axle and its tires, while too little weight up front can leave the steering axle too light to steer safely. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
Too little weight on the driving axles gives poor traction and lets the drive wheels spin easily. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
Uneven side-to-side loading can tip a trailer over, especially in turns; to prevent a rollover, take turns slowly and keep cargo close to the ground. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
A load-distributing hitch spreads the tongue load across all axles of the tow vehicle and trailer to steady the tow vehicle, and is used for heavier utility, boat and travel trailers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
When hitching a ball coupler, the ball must be seated firmly in the coupler, the coupler safety latch secured down, and the safety chains attached and crossed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
The ball mount must be locked into the tow vehicle's receiver with its pin and clip or other locking device, and the electric lines must be seated, locked and free of tangles or dragging. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
A fifth-wheel hitch mounts in a pickup bed and couples to the trailer's kingpin; it is very stable but uses most of the bed and needs the space behind it kept clear for turns. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A02
Before backing under a fifth-wheel trailer, lock the trailer brakes, and after the jaws close around the kingpin, make sure the locking lever is locked or the coupling is not properly seated. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A03
A coupled fifth wheel must have no gap between the upper and lower coupling, the trailer must sit flat on the skid plate, and the plate must be greased as required. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A03
Test the hitch by pulling gently forward in low gear against the locked trailer brakes, then look at the connection; chains and electric lines should be secure with enough slack for turns. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A03
On a long trip, re-inspect the trailer and its load-securing devices within the first 50 miles, then again after 3 hours or 150 miles of driving, and ideally at every break. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A03
Signalling your intentions while towing is required by law as well as being important for safety. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A03
Empty trucks actually need longer stopping distances than loaded ones, because they have less traction and can bounce and lock their wheels. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A04
When backing a single vehicle you turn the top of the steering wheel toward where you want to go, but when backing a trailer you turn it the opposite way, then follow the trailer once it starts turning. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A04
Backing is always dangerous, so avoid it when you can, and park so you can pull forward when leaving. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A04
Before backing a trailer, get out and walk around to check your path and clearance to the sides and overhead, then back as slowly as possible. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A04
If the trailer starts drifting off course while backing, correct at once by turning the top of the steering wheel toward the drift. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A04
Back and turn toward the driver's side whenever possible, even if it means circling the block, because backing toward the right side is very dangerous. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F27 | anchor: A04
Use a helper standing near the rear where you can see them, and agree on hand signals, including one for stop, before you begin backing. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F28 | anchor: A04
On a right turn that needs extra room, turn wide only as you finish the turn and keep the trailer's rear near the curb; do not swing wide left at the start, which invites drivers to pass on your right. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F29 | anchor: A04
If you must cross into oncoming traffic to turn, give oncoming vehicles room to pass or stop, but do not back up for them. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F30 | anchor: A05
On a left turn with a trailer, reach the center of the intersection before turning, because turning early lets off-tracking swing the vehicle's left side into other traffic. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F31 | anchor: A05
With two left-turn lanes, always use the right-hand one, since starting from the inside lane may force you to swing right into drivers you cannot see. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F32 | anchor: A05
A towing rig accelerates slowly, so it needs a much bigger gap to cross or enter traffic, more so when heavily loaded; be sure you can clear the road before traffic arrives. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F33 | anchor: A05
Do not trust posted heights at bridges and overpasses, since repaving or packed snow may have lowered the clearance, and an empty trailer rides higher than a loaded one. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F34 | anchor: A05
If you doubt you can fit under an object, go slowly, and if still unsure, take another route; low bridges may not be marked. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F35 | anchor: A05
Heavily loaded vehicles have little ground clearance, so cross raised railroad tracks and drainage channels carefully to avoid getting hung up or dragging. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F36 | anchor: A06
In a combination of towed vehicles, the heaviest vehicle must always be placed first behind the towing vehicle, with the lighter one at the rear. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-F37 | anchor: A06
Trailers have a crack-the-whip effect, caused by rearward amplification and worse with more trailers, which can flip a trailer during a quick lane change, so steer gently and smoothly. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-F38 | anchor: A07
If trailer wheels lock and the trailer starts to skid, release the brakes to regain traction, and do not use the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig, since trailer braking caused the skid. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0074]

Misconceptions: an empty trailer or truck does not stop shorter, it usually needs more distance; backing a trailer is not steered like a car, the wheel goes the opposite way; a posted bridge height is not a guarantee; the trailer hand brake does not cure a trailer skid, it causes one; swinging wide left before a right turn is the wrong move.
Mnemonics: ten thousand pounds and seventy feet for Class C; heavy low, heavy forward; fifty miles, then three hours or one-fifty; back to the driver's side; brakes off to stop the slide.
Glossary: GVWR means gross vehicle weight rating; GCWR means gross combination weight rating; tongue means the front bar of a trailer that carries the coupler; kingpin means the pin on a fifth-wheel trailer that locks into the hitch jaws; off-tracking means rear wheels or a trailer cutting inside the path of the front wheels; jackknife means a trailer swinging around toward the tow vehicle; rearward amplification means the whipping that grows toward the last trailer.
Dynamic facts: Class C towing limits and endorsement requirements are set by law and the study guide lives on the DMV website, so confirm them against current Nevada DMV material.
